title: Existence of an infinite family of substrates satisfying all the postulates of integrated information theory, exclusion included, with arbitrarily large integrated information
summary: For infinitely many sizes we exhibit a cycle of binary units, each taking the exclusive-or of itself and its two clockwise neighbours, that is a complex in every state, no proper subsystem being more integrated, and whose integrated information grows as two raised to a power quadratic in the number of units.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs binary XOR cycles of certain sizes that form complexes (maximally integrated subsystems) in every state, with integrated information growing doubly-exponentially (2^(quadratic)) in the number of units.
AI.motivation: Integrated information theory (IIT) seeks to quantify integration, but explicit examples with extreme integration are rare; the work likely aims to demonstrate that simple binary XOR systems can exhibit vastly growing integrated information and be complexes in all states.
AI.method: Constructs a cycle of binary units where each unit applies XOR to itself and its two clockwise neighbours, then analyzes integration across states; for infinitely many cycle sizes it is shown to be a complex in every state (no proper subsystem more integrated).
AI.result: For infinitely many sizes, the constructed cycle is a complex in every state, and its integrated information scales as 2 raised to a power quadratic in the number of units.
AI.conclusion: Simple XOR-based binary cycles can achieve maximal integration in all states with super-exponentially (doubly-exponentially in exponent form) large integrated information for infinitely many sizes.

title: Clustering without clusters: the meta-criterion and centroid reliability mistake continuous dynamics for discrete states
summary: Microstate analysis starts with clustering and the meta-criterion is a heuristic to find an optimum cluster number. We address the following questions: (i) what number is found for non-cluster-forming dynamical systems, (ii) do centroids fall in random attractor regions, (iii) do EEG topographies form clusters or a single connected structure in sensor space? We find that (i) the meta-criterion suggests spurious optimal cluster numbers (4-8) with high confidence on different attractor geometries, (ii) cluster centroids reliably fall in the same attractor regions, (iii) topological analysis of dynamical systems and resting-state EEG suggests that all form a single connected structure in their respective phase space, not clusters. We conclude that the meta-criterion should be used with caution and its results should not be taken as representing a ground truth. Cluster numbers deviating from the meta-criterion should not be discarded. A more far-reaching implication is that evidence for the existence of clusters in resting-state EEG data is still lacking. Microstate clustering may correspond to the partitioning of a single connected structure.

AI.tldr: The meta-criterion used in microstate analysis suggests spurious optimal cluster numbers (4-8) even for non-cluster-forming systems, and resting-state EEG likely forms a single connected structure rather than distinct clusters.
AI.motivation: Microstate analysis relies on clustering and the meta-criterion to determine an optimum cluster number, but it is unclear whether this criterion and the resulting cluster solutions reflect genuine clusters or artifacts, especially for systems that do not inherently form clusters.
AI.method: The authors tested the meta-criterion on non-cluster-forming dynamical systems with different attractor geometries, examined whether cluster centroids fall in random attractor regions, and applied topological analysis to dynamical systems and resting-state EEG in sensor space.
AI.result: The meta-criterion suggested spurious optimal cluster numbers (4-8) with high confidence across different attractor geometries; cluster centroids reliably fell in the same attractor regions; and topological analysis indicated that both dynamical systems and resting-state EEG form a single connected structure in their phase space, not clusters.
AI.conclusion: The meta-criterion should be used with caution and its results should not be treated as ground truth; cluster numbers deviating from it should not be discarded. More importantly, evidence for the existence of clusters in resting-state EEG is still lacking, and microstate clustering may merely partition a single connected structure.

title: Causal discovery identifies pathways linking physical activity to dementia risk in the UK BioBank
summary: Physical Activity (PA) is consistently associated with lower risk of dementia, yet the mechanism linking PA to dementia prevention remain incomopletely understood. Here, we integrate large language model (LLM)-guided causal discovery with mediation analysis in 42,293 older adults aged 60 years or older from the UK Biobank to systematically identify pathways connecting objectively measured moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) to dementia risk. Across behavioral, psychological, functional, and clinical domains, causal discovery consistently identified interconnected pathways linking higher MVPA to lower dementia risk through depression, functional capacity, smoking behavior, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, and brain injury. Chain mediation analyses further identified depression as a central pathway, accounting for 15.1% of the overall association between MVPA and dementia risk. Sex-stratified analyses revealed distinct mechanistic patterns, with females exhibiting predominantly metabolic and functional pathways, while males showed behavioral and cardiometabolic cascades involving smoking and cardiovascular disease. Together, these findings suggest that the protective association between PA and dementia is mediated through interconnected behavioral, psychological, and cardiometabolic processes rather than a single pathway. Depression emerged as a prominent and potentially modifiable pathway, highlighting opportunities for integrating dementia prevention strategies that combine PA promotion with mental health and cardiovascular risk management.

AI.tldr: Using LLM-guided causal discovery and mediation analysis in 42,293 UK Biobank older adults, this study identifies interconnected behavioral, psychological, and cardiometabolic pathways linking moderate-to-vigorous physical activity to lower dementia risk, with depression as a central mediator (15.1%).
AI.motivation: Physical activity is consistently associated with lower dementia risk, but the mechanisms linking PA to dementia prevention remain incompletely understood.
AI.method: Integrates LLM-guided causal discovery with mediation analysis in 42,293 adults aged 60+ from the UK Biobank, using objectively measured moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) and dementia risk, across behavioral, psychological, functional, and clinical domains. Includes chain mediation and sex-stratified analyses.
AI.result: Causal discovery identified interconnected pathways linking higher MVPA to lower dementia risk through depression, functional capacity, smoking, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, and brain injury. Depression was a central mediator, accounting for 15.1% of the overall association. Sex-stratified analyses showed distinct patterns: females predominantly metabolic and functional pathways; males behavioral and cardiometabolic cascades involving smoking and cardiovascular disease.
AI.conclusion: The protective association between PA and dementia is mediated through interconnected behavioral, psychological, and cardiometabolic processes rather than a single pathway. Depression is a prominent, potentially modifiable pathway, supporting dementia prevention strategies combining PA promotion with mental health and cardiovascular risk management.

title: A coupled geometric surface and surface reaction-diffusion framework for modelling nuclear mechanics during confined cell migration
summary: Confined cell migration is governed by nuclear and cellular deformation. In this work, we formulate a two-dimensional mathematical framework in which the cell and nuclear membranes are represented as evolving closed surfaces governed by force-balance laws incorporating surface tension, bending elasticity, and external mechanical interactions. Nuclear mechanics depends on several factors, including chromatin organization and compaction, which are regulated by epigenetic modifications. Molecular regulation at the nuclear periphery is described by a surface reaction-diffusion system posed on the evolving nuclear surface. We apply this coupled framework to an experimentally characterized lung cancer cell model in which the balance between the enzymes SETDB1 and SUV39H1 regulates the peripheral deposition of H3K9me3. Using experimentally measured mechanical parameters, we represent control (Ctrl) and SETDB1 knockout (SETDB1 KO) conditions, which display distinct H3K9me3 distributions, especially at the nuclear periphery. Numerical solutions obtained using the evolving surface finite element method qualitatively reproduce the changes in nuclear mechanics as well as part of the experimentally observed increase in the entry time in SETDB1 KO cells. The model therefore reproduces the direction of the experimental observations, while the residual difference between simulated and measured entry times indicates that the cellular response is multifactorial.

AI.tldr: A 2D computational framework couples cell/nuclear membrane mechanics with surface reaction-diffusion of epigenetic markers to study confined migration, applied to lung cancer cells where SETDB1/SUV39H1 balance controls H3K9me3 and nuclear mechanics.
AI.motivation: Confined cell migration is governed by nuclear and cellular deformation, but how epigenetic regulation of the nuclear periphery (e.g., H3K9me3 distribution via SETDB1/SUV39H1) feeds back into nuclear mechanics remains poorly captured in a unified model.
AI.method: A two-dimensional mathematical framework represents cell and nuclear membranes as evolving closed surfaces governed by force-balance laws with surface tension, bending elasticity, and external mechanical interactions. A surface reaction-diffusion system on the evolving nuclear surface describes molecular regulation at the periphery. The framework is applied to an experimentally characterized lung cancer cell model comparing control and SETDB1 knockout conditions, solved numerically via the evolving surface finite element method using experimentally measured mechanical parameters.
AI.result: Numerical solutions qualitatively reproduce the changes in nuclear mechanics and part of the experimentally observed increase in entry time in SETDB1 KO cells. The model reproduces the direction of experimental observations.
AI.conclusion: The model captures the qualitative trend of SETDB1 KO effects on nuclear mechanics and confined migration entry time; the residual gap between simulated and measured entry times indicates the cellular response is multifactorial.

title: Generalizable single-cell perturbation response prediction using energy-guided flow matching
summary: Predicting phenotypic and transcriptional responses to perturbations at single-cell resolution provides a powerful tool for probing biological systems. However, existing methods typically rely on fixed mappings learned during training, making it challenging to calibrate distribution shifts or adapt to novel perturbation conditions during inference. Here, we present scEGFlow, an energy-guided flow matching framework that dynamically bridges control and perturbed cellular states. scEGFlow models continuous transitions from control cell populations to perturbed states using conditional flow matching. It then applies condition-specific energy gradients to correct and steer these predictions, enabling flexible adjustments without retraining the flow model. Evaluations across benchmarks spanning imaging phenotypes and transcriptomic profiles show that scEGFlow outperforms existing methods in reconstructing response distributions under both seen and unseen perturbation conditions, faithfully preserving cellular manifold geometry and population heterogeneity. This advantage is notable when adapting to new conditions with only a few measured cells, consistently improving prediction accuracy. Furthermore, scEGFlow accurately recapitulates perturbation-induced up- and down-regulation patterns across consensus gene expression signatures, where energy guidance improves the agreement between predicted and observed regulatory directions. Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that scEGFlow provides a modular, generalizable, and steerable solution for single-cell perturbation modeling. By grounding generative flows in learned biological landscapes, this architecture establishes a new computational paradigm for navigating and manipulating cellular behavior in silico.

AI.tldr: scEGFlow is an energy-guided flow matching framework that dynamically bridges control and perturbed cellular states, outperforming existing methods in predicting single-cell perturbation responses under seen and unseen conditions.
AI.motivation: Predicting phenotypic and transcriptional responses to perturbations at single-cell resolution is powerful for probing biological systems, but existing methods rely on fixed mappings learned during training, making it hard to calibrate distribution shifts or adapt to novel perturbation conditions during inference.
AI.method: scEGFlow models continuous transitions from control cell populations to perturbed states using conditional flow matching, then applies condition-specific energy gradients to correct and steer these predictions, enabling flexible adjustment without retraining the flow model.
AI.result: Across benchmarks spanning imaging phenotypes and transcriptomic profiles, scEGFlow outperforms existing methods in reconstructing response distributions under seen and unseen perturbations, preserving cellular manifold geometry and heterogeneity. It adapts well with only a few measured cells and accurately recapitulates up-/down-regulation patterns, with energy guidance improving agreement between predicted and observed regulatory directions.
AI.conclusion: scEGFlow provides a modular, generalizable, and steerable solution for single-cell perturbation modeling, establishing a new computational paradigm for navigating and manipulating cellular behavior in silico by grounding generative flows in learned biological landscapes.

title: Toward Controlling Biology with Language:Offline Learning of Prompt-Conditioned Interventions for Cells, Organoids, and Biobots
summary: Artificial intelligence increasingly serves as a natural-language interface to complex technical systems, letting people accomplish sophisticated tasks by describing what they want rather than specifying how to do it. Extending this interface to living systems is harder: unlike code or images, a biological intervention has no closed-form linguistic meaning, and the paired language-intervention-outcome data needed to learn such a mapping is expensive to collect, since each example requires its own wet-lab experiment. One way around this is to treat an existing archive of interventions and their already-observed outcomes as a fixed, offline dataset, and use a vision-language model to judge, without any new experiments, whether an archived outcome matches a natural-language description. But whether that judgment is reliable enough to train a language-to-intervention mapping on -- without new experiments and without human validation -- has remained unclear. Here we show that a natural-language interface for a living organism -- a xenobot, a synthetic multicellular construct with no nervous system -- can be learned entirely offline this way, using a vision-language model's own judgment as the sole training reward: an instruction is mapped to the intervention already on record as producing the described behavior. This mapping generalizes to entirely new instructions, evaluated against archive data withheld from training (80.0% held-out accuracy vs a $66.7% chance baseline, matching a network trained directly on ground-truth labels).

AI.tldr: A language-to-intervention interface for xenobots (synthetic multicellular constructs without a nervous system) can be learned entirely offline using a vision-language model's judgment as the sole training reward, achieving 80.0% held-out accuracy versus 66.7% chance.
AI.motivation: AI is increasingly a natural-language interface to complex systems, but extending this to living systems is hard: a biological intervention has no closed-form linguistic meaning, and paired language-intervention-outcome data is expensive since each example needs its own wet-lab experiment.
AI.method: Treat an existing archive of interventions and already-observed outcomes as a fixed offline dataset. Use a vision-language model to judge, without new experiments, whether an archived outcome matches a natural-language description. This judgment serves as the sole training reward to learn a mapping from instructions to the recorded intervention that produced the described behavior.
AI.result: The learned language-to-intervention mapping generalizes to entirely new instructions, evaluated against archive data withheld from training: 80.0% held-out accuracy versus a 66.7% chance baseline, matching a network trained directly on ground-truth labels.
AI.conclusion: A reliable natural-language interface for a living organism (a xenobot) can be learned entirely offline via a vision-language model's own judgment, without new experiments and without human validation.

title: Generating eukaryotic reference genome assemblies: Earth BioGenome Project quality standards and recommendations
summary: Reference genome assemblies are foundational resources across the biological sciences as they begin to expose the fundamental building blocks of each species and the molecular toolkits vital for adaptation and survival. High-quality genomes enable insights into evolution, facilitate ecosystem monitoring and protection and conservation of species, access to new biomaterials and biomedicine, advances in agri- and aquaculture, and support planetary health. The amount of information gathered from a species' genome assembly is directly dependent on its quality. However, different sequencing technologies and software solutions generate a wide range of quality outcomes. Here, the Earth BioGenome Project's Sequencing and Assembly committee, together with a large community of researchers performing eukaryote sequencing and assembly, outlines quality standards for a "reference" assembly and formulates recommendations to ensure these standards are met.

AI.tldr: The Earth BioGenome Project's Sequencing and Assembly committee, with a broad community of eukaryote researchers, outlines quality standards for a "reference" genome assembly and provides recommendations to achieve them.
AI.motivation: Reference genome assemblies are foundational to biology, enabling insights into evolution, ecosystem monitoring, conservation, biomaterials, biomedicine, agri/aquaculture, and planetary health. The value derived from a genome depends directly on its quality, but different sequencing technologies and software produce widely varying quality outcomes, creating a need for agreed standards.
AI.method: A community-driven effort: the Earth BioGenome Project's Sequencing and Assembly committee, joined by a large community of researchers performing eukaryote sequencing and assembly, defines quality standards for a "reference" assembly and formulates recommendations to meet them.
AI.result: The paper articulates quality standards for a "reference" genome assembly and presents recommendations designed to ensure these standards are met.
AI.conclusion: Establishing and adhering to these community-defined quality standards is essential to maximize the scientific, societal, and planetary benefits of reference genome assemblies.

title: Multimodal reasoning for broadly neutralizing antibody discovery from label-free human B cell repertoires across virus families
summary: Discovering broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) from human natural immune repertoires remains a fundamental challenge in immunology, hindered by: the extreme rarity of bnAb, incomplete understanding of their cellular origins across pathogens, and the inability of existing computational tools to generalize across emerging viral threats. Here we present ImmuneAgent, a closed-loop AI system that integrates multimodal reasoning with continual meta-learning and wet-lab feedback to overcome these barriers. Applied to screen the natural BCR repertoires from vaccinated or infected cohorts, the system achieves a ~55% neutralization antibody discovery rate (60 of 110 cloned candidates) and a ~11% bnAb yield (12 of 110), substantially outperforming a state-of-the-art sequence-based neutralization predictor or cofolding models evaluated at the same cloning budget. Five ImmuneAgent-discovered antibodies conferred 100% in vivo protection against lethal influenza challenge, comparable to the clinical-stage therapeutic MEDI8852. The system recovered the cellular and structural determinants of bnAb activity and identified FCRL5+CD27+ atypical memory B cells as a conserved bnAb reservoir and hydrophobic interface enrichment as a cross-viral structural signature, which generalized to unseen antigens, discovering human metapneumovirus (hMPV) cross-neutralizing and human papillomavirus (HPV)-neutralizing antibodies without antigen-specific sorting. These results validate that ImmuneAgent is a generalizable framework for rapid therapeutic antibody discovery against emerging viral threats.

AI.tldr: ImmuneAgent is a closed-loop AI system combining multimodal reasoning, continual meta-learning, and wet-lab feedback to discover broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) from natural immune repertoires, achieving high discovery yields and generalizing to unseen viral threats.
AI.motivation: Discovering bnAbs from human natural immune repertoires is hindered by their extreme rarity, incomplete understanding of their cellular origins across pathogens, and the inability of existing computational tools to generalize across emerging viral threats.
AI.method: ImmuneAgent integrates multimodal reasoning with continual meta-learning and wet-lab feedback in a closed loop, applied to screen natural BCR repertoires from vaccinated or infected cohorts.
AI.result: Achieved ~55% neutralization antibody discovery rate (60/110) and ~11% bnAb yield (12/110), outperforming sequence-based predictors and cofolding models. Five antibodies conferred 100% in vivo protection against lethal influenza, comparable to MEDI8852. Identified FCRL5+CD27+ atypical memory B cells as a conserved bnAb reservoir and hydrophobic interface enrichment as a cross-viral structural signature, generalizing to hMPV and HPV cross-neutralizing antibodies without antigen-specific sorting.
AI.conclusion: ImmuneAgent is a generalizable framework for rapid therapeutic antibody discovery against emerging viral threats.

title: Contrastive Neural Embeddings Reveal Individual Traits Beyond Conversational Role
summary: Contrastive representation learning is increasingly used to recover low-dimensional structure from neural recordings, but its output is typically validated by decoding accuracy rather than by the geometry of the manifold it produces. We apply CEBRA to EEG recorded from dyads in conversation, and analyze the resulting embedding, which training constrains to the 2D sphere. Labels describing the dyads, including the absolute difference between partners' autism-quotient scores, decode well above chance (0.77 against a 0.55 majority baseline for binary AQ magnitude; 0.44 against 0.25 for the six-class $|Δ$AQ$|$ partition). However, the two permutation controls have notable differences in results: permuting labels over a frozen embedding yields p = 0.001, whereas retraining the encoder under each permutation yields p = 0.50. Only the latter tests the label rather than the geometry. Consistent with this, spherical mixture structure and per-class dispersion track identity rather than autism trait differences in dyads; frequency-band and non-oscillatory activity ablation controls do not change the results. However, participant-level model does separate from its identity-aware null (p = 0.0099) while speaker-versus-listener role analysis performs at chance in the same embedding, indicating a manifold organized by individual -- and, in contrast with current neurolinguistics models, almost invariant to speaking vs. listening. Based on these results, we suggest that retraining-based nulls should be the default for grouped-data contrastive embeddings.

AI.tldr: CEBRA embeddings of dyadic EEG decode labels well, but geometry-based validation shows the manifold is organized by individual identity, not autism traits; retraining-based permutation nulls should be the default for grouped-data contrastive embeddings.
AI.motivation: Contrastive representation learning is increasingly used to recover low-dimensional structure from neural recordings, yet its output is usually validated by decoding accuracy rather than by the geometry of the learned manifold. The paper argues decoding accuracy alone can mislead about what structure a contrastive embedding actually captures.
AI.method: Applied CEBRA to EEG from conversing dyads, with training constraining the embedding to the 2D sphere. Compared two permutation controls: (1) permuting labels over a frozen embedding, and (2) retraining the encoder under each permutation. Also used spherical mixture structure, per-class dispersion, frequency-band and non-oscillatory activity ablations, a participant-level model test, and speaker-vs-listener role analysis.
AI.result: Labels decoded well above chance (0.77 vs 0.55 majority baseline for binary AQ magnitude; 0.44 vs 0.25 for six-class |ΔAQ|). But the two nulls diverged: frozen-embedding permutation gave p = 0.001, while retraining under permutation gave p = 0.50. Spherical mixture structure and per-class dispersion tracked identity rather than autism trait differences; ablations did not change results. Participant-level model separated from its identity-aware null (p = 0.0099), while speaker-vs-listener role performed at chance.
AI.conclusion: The manifold is organized by individual identity and is nearly invariant to speaking vs listening, contrasting with current neurolinguistics models. Retraining-based nulls should be the default for validating grouped-data contrastive embeddings, since only they test the label rather than the geometry.

title: Autoregressive Frontier Expansion: Growing Trees with Graph Machine Learning
summary: Tree-like branching structures are common in nature, from botanical trees to neurons, blood vessels and respiratory trees. Their branching shape often reflects function, making structural modelling central to understanding how these systems work. Because acquiring real-world 3D data is often expensive or infeasible, realistic generative models are valuable for simulation and data augmentation. Existing morphology-specific models either constrain how topology is generated or rely on hand-tuned, mechanistic procedures. Generic 3D graph generators, by contrast, do not exploit or enforce the structure of trees. We propose Autoregressive Frontier Expansion, a generative framework that constructs trees through an iterative expansion process, simulating the biological growth of real trees. At each step, a flow-matching model parameterised by an SO(2)-equivariant GNN expands the frontier by predicting whether each active branch bifurcates or terminates. We evaluate our method on cortical neurons and botanical trees in unconditional, class-conditioned, and morphology-guided generation. Across both domains, the generated morphologies agree closely with the reference distributions and, in conditional experiments, with the specified targets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Autoregressive Frontier Expansion, a generative framework for tree-like branching structures that iteratively expands a frontier using a flow-matching model parameterized by an SO(2)-equivariant GNN to predict branch bifurcation or termination, validated on neurons and botanical trees.
AI.motivation: Real-world 3D tree data is expensive or infeasible to acquire, so realistic generative models are valuable. Existing morphology-specific models constrain topology generation or rely on hand-tuned mechanisms, while generic 3D graph generators fail to exploit/enforce tree structure.
AI.method: Autoregressive Frontier Expansion: an iterative expansion process mimicking biological growth. At each step, a flow-matching model parameterised by an SO(2)-equivariant GNN expands the frontier, predicting whether each active branch bifurcates or terminates.
AI.result: Evaluated on cortical neurons and botanical trees across unconditional, class-conditioned, and morphology-guided generation. Generated morphologies closely match reference distributions and, in conditional experiments, the specified targets.
AI.conclusion: The framework produces realistic tree-like branching structures that align with reference distributions and controllable targets, offering a valuable tool for simulation and data augmentation across both neural and botanical domains.

title: Traveling waves, phase separation and pattern formation in the active stepping stone model
summary: Selective advantage leads to the proliferation of a species into an ecosystem. On the other hand, self-propulsion can lead to dynamic clustering of individuals. To analyze the intricate effects produced by such competing processes, we introduce a minimal model for a proliferating active population, where run-and-tumble migration is combined with a stochastic birth-death process. Beginning with the microscopic dynamics of the particles, we derive the corresponding hydrodynamic equations and validate them through numerical simulations. We demonstrate that the inclusion of activity leads to the emergence of novel morphological patterns, which are sensitive to the specific rules governing migration. Furthermore, we show that activity significantly alters the characteristics of invasion waves, increasing their propagation speed. However, beyond a threshold, excessive activity disrupts the wave-like nature of the invasion process. We also extend our study to two dimensions and analyze the instabilities that lead to pattern formation in such systems.

AI.tldr: A minimal model combining run-and-tumble migration with a stochastic birth-death process shows that activity reshapes proliferation dynamics, creating novel patterns and faster but eventually destabilized invasion waves.
AI.motivation: Selective advantage drives species proliferation, while self-propulsion causes dynamic clustering. The interplay of these competing processes is poorly understood and needs a tractable framework.
AI.method: Starting from microscopic particle dynamics, the authors derive hydrodynamic equations for a proliferating active population and validate them against numerical simulations; the study is extended to two dimensions with instability analysis.
AI.result: Activity induces novel morphological patterns sensitive to migration rules. It increases invasion wave speed, but beyond a threshold excessive activity disrupts wave-like invasion. In 2D, instabilities drive pattern formation.
AI.conclusion: The interplay of activity and proliferation produces rich, rule-dependent pattern formation and qualitatively modifies invasion dynamics, offering a minimal framework for proliferating active matter.

title: NeuroLens: Learning Latent Embeddings of Neural Semantics from Chronic Recordings
summary: Understanding how neural activity represents higher-order cognition and how these representations evolve over time has long been a central pursuit in neuroscience. However, current analytical tools cannot easily distinguish representational plasticity from recording instability in chronic neural recordings. Here, we introduce NeuroLens (Latent Embeddings of Neural Semantics), a self-supervised model based on the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) framework that learns denoised, semantically informative latents from chronic neural recordings. An adaptive encoder maps changing neural populations into a common latent space, while a temporal predictor learns structure that supports prediction of future latent states. By predicting in latent space, NeuroLens captures temporally predictable structure and reduces sensitivity to transient, recording-specific variability. Across chronic intracortical data in mice and humans, the learned representations improve decoding of decision-making and semantic task variables. Multi-day pretraining enables generalization to future sessions, rapid few-shot adaptation to unseen neural populations, and more stable decoding over time than state-of-the-art baselines. Together, these results establish NeuroLens as a new paradigm for studying how neural representations change during learning and over long timescales.

AI.tldr: NeuroLens, a self-supervised JEPA-based model, learns denoised semantic latents from chronic neural recordings, separating representational plasticity from recording instability and enabling stable cross-session decoding.
AI.motivation: Neuroscience aims to understand how neural activity represents higher-order cognition and evolves over time, but existing analytical tools cannot easily distinguish representational plasticity from recording instability in chronic neural recordings.
AI.method: NeuroLens (Latent Embeddings of Neural Semantics) is a self-supervised model based on the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA). An adaptive encoder maps changing neural populations into a common latent space, and a temporal predictor learns structure supporting prediction of future latent states. Predicting in latent space captures temporally predictable structure while reducing sensitivity to transient, recording-specific variability.
AI.result: Across chronic intracortical data in mice and humans, learned representations improve decoding of decision-making and semantic task variables. Multi-day pretraining enables generalization to future sessions, rapid few-shot adaptation to unseen neural populations, and more stable decoding over time than state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: NeuroLens establishes a new paradigm for studying how neural representations change during learning and over long timescales.

title: Response Variability and Stability in Human Reasoning
comment: Accepted as full paper with talk at the 48th Annual Conference of the Cognitive Science Society (CogSci 2026). This version contains minor revisions
summary: Understanding how humans reason -- and how reasoning responses vary across tasks and individuals -- remains a core challenge for modeling and explanation in cognitive science. We investigate the stability of response patterns within reasoners and whether variation in these patterns can be used to predict learning effects. We introduce a formal, geometry-based method to quantify distances between individual reasoning patterns and their internal variability, grounded in heuristic theories. The proposed framework is tested against experimental data via generalized linear mixed-effects models and clustering, where we find that our proposed variation measure interacts with correctness to predict performance gains. Moreover, we find that reasoning patterns are stable over time within the same reasoner. The method is general enough to be applied to other reasoning domains.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a geometry-based method to quantify distances between individual reasoning patterns and their internal variability, testing whether pattern variation predicts learning effects using experimental data and mixed-effects models with clustering.
AI.motivation: Understanding how humans reason and how reasoning responses vary across tasks and individuals remains a core challenge for modeling and explanation in cognitive science.
AI.method: A formal, geometry-based method grounded in heuristic theories is proposed to quantify distances between individual reasoning patterns and their internal variability. The framework is tested against experimental data using generalized linear mixed-effects models and clustering.
AI.result: The proposed variation measure interacts with correctness to predict performance gains. Additionally, reasoning patterns are found to be stable over time within the same reasoner.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning patterns are stable over time within individuals, and the variation measure helps predict learning effects. The method is general enough to be applied to other reasoning domains.

title: Broken scale symmetries in undercomplete linear autoencoders
comment: NeurIPS 2026 Symmetry and Geometry in Neural Representations Workshop
summary: Neural network loss landscapes have many symmetries, which are preserved by gradient flow but broken by finite-stepsize stochastic gradient descent (SGD). A canonical example of such a symmetry is scale in homogeneous networks: one can scale up the parameters in one layer and down in the next without changing the network output. Previous work has documented cases in which SGD breaks this symmetry in favor of balancing gradient noise or minimizing fluctuations. Here, we show that the solution geometry of undercomplete linear autoencoders instead selects a preferred sign for scale drift: on the PCA solution manifold, SGD favors large decoder weights. This directed scale drift occurs on a slow timescale, and its dynamics admit an analytically-tractable effective description. However, it cannot continue indefinitely: increasing scale eventually drives the dynamics towards a finite-stepsize stability boundary. The resulting solutions are sharper than a balanced baseline in the sense of the maximum eigenvalue of the loss Hessian, but different sharpness measures can move in opposing directions. Thus, undercomplete autoencoders give a concrete illustration of how loss geometry can convert residual gradient noise into directed motion along a manifold of functionally-equivalent solutions.

AI.tldr: SGD on undercomplete linear autoencoders breaks scale symmetry in a directed way: it drifts toward large decoder weights on the PCA solution manifold, until reaching a finite-stepsize stability boundary, yielding solutions sharper than a balanced baseline.
AI.motivation: Neural network loss landscapes have many symmetries (e.g., scale symmetry in homogeneous networks) preserved by gradient flow but broken by finite-stepsize SGD. Prior work showed SGD breaks scale symmetry to balance gradient noise or minimize fluctuations, but it is unclear whether solution geometry can instead select a preferred direction (sign) for scale drift.
AI.method: Analytical study of scale drift dynamics for undercomplete linear autoencoders under finite-stepsize SGD, using an analytically-tractable effective description. Examines behavior on the PCA solution manifold and identifies a finite-stepsize stability boundary.
AI.result: On the PCA solution manifold, SGD favors large decoder weights—a directed scale drift occurring on a slow timescale. This drift cannot continue indefinitely: increasing scale drives the dynamics toward a finite-stepsize stability boundary. Resulting solutions are sharper than a balanced baseline by max Hessian eigenvalue, though different sharpness measures can move in opposing directions.
AI.conclusion: Undercomplete autoencoders concretely illustrate how loss geometry can convert residual gradient noise into directed motion along a manifold of functionally-equivalent solutions.

title: Does a mortality schedule need a Makeham term? Calibrating the likelihood-ratio test
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Code and reproducibility materials: https://github.com/scpatricio/Makeham_LRT
summary: Whether a fitted mortality model needs a Makeham term, the non-negative constant representing background mortality, is commonly decided with a likelihood-ratio test. Because the constant cannot be negative, testing its absence places the parameter on the boundary of its range, and the usual chi-squared calibration does not apply. Assuming independent Poisson death counts and standard regularity conditions, we show that when the constant is the only parameter on a boundary the statistic converges to an equal mixture of a point mass at zero and a chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom, so that at the 5% level the critical value is 2.71 rather than 3.84. We give conditions under which the correction holds for Makeham models, verify them for Gompertz-Makeham and gamma-Gompertz-Makeham, and quantify the information the data carry about the constant, which fixes the local power of the test, the smallest term it can detect, and how fast detectability falls as the age window narrows. When a gamma-frailty variance is estimated and its true value is also zero, the limit is no longer a chi-squared mixture and the usual correction rejects too often. Monte Carlo experiments show that the conventional cutoff rejects at half the nominal level, that a correctly calibrated test can still miss a term at its own detection threshold in most samples, and that excess rejections under an estimated zero frailty variance persist as exposure grows.

AI.tldr: The paper corrects the likelihood-ratio test for a Makeham background-mortality term, whose parameter lies on the boundary, showing the statistic converges to a 0-chi-squared(1) mixture with critical value 2.71 at 5%, and examines when this fails.
AI.motivation: Deciding whether a mortality model needs a Makeham term is usually done with a likelihood-ratio test, but since the constant cannot be negative its absence puts the parameter on the boundary of its range, invalidating the standard chi-squared calibration.
AI.method: Assuming independent Poisson death counts and standard regularity conditions, the authors derive the asymptotic distribution of the test statistic when the constant is the only boundary parameter, give conditions under which the correction holds for Makeham models, verify them for Gompertz-Makeham and gamma-Gompertz-Makeham, quantify the information the data carry about the constant, and run Monte Carlo experiments.
AI.result: The statistic converges to an equal mixture of a point mass at zero and a chi-squared with one degree of freedom, giving a 5% critical value of 2.71 instead of 3.84. When a gamma-frailty variance is also estimated with true value zero, the limit is no longer a chi-squared mixture and the usual correction rejects too often. Simulations show the conventional cutoff rejects at half the nominal level, a correctly calibrated test can miss a term at its detection threshold in most samples, and excess rejections persist as exposure grows.
AI.conclusion: The correct boundary-aware calibration (critical value 2.71) should replace the standard 3.84 cutoff for testing a Makeham term, but the mixture result breaks down when an additional boundary parameter such as a zero gamma-frailty variance is present, producing persistent over-rejection.

title: RNADyn: A Benchmark for Generating and Understanding RNA Dynamics
summary: Ribonucleic acid (RNA) functions through conformational changes that are not fully captured by static structures. However, large-scale standardized RNA dynamics data remain limited, and existing approaches typically treat trajectory generation and dynamics understanding as separate objectives. Here, we introduce RNADynBench, a standardized RNA molecular dynamics (MD) benchmark with 2585 quality-controlled 100-ns all-atom trajectories and leakage-controlled splits. Building on RNADynBench, we develop RNADynNet, a unified model for RNA dynamics learning that uses a shared backbone for both trajectory generation and dynamics fingerprint extraction from a single conformer. It combines coordinate denoising, single-frame-to-trajectory alignment, and physical grounding to connect all-atom trajectory generation with dynamics representation learning. Physical grounding improves both generated dynamics and the physical information recoverable from these fingerprints. Across both test sets, including the high-flexibility challenge set, the generated trajectories achieve RMSF correlations of 0.875 and 0.766, while single-conformer predictions show comparable agreement with MD-derived dynamics. RNADynBench and RNADynNet together establish a benchmark and unified modeling framework for generating and understanding RNA dynamics.
